clinicalPearls: X-linked recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia mapped to the proximal long arm of the X chromosome (Xq11.2-q23); it predominantly affects males, while heterozygous females are usually unaffected or only subtly symptomatic.

Occurs in both pure and complicated forms; the complicated phenotype is characterised by cognitive impairment, motor aphasia or dysarthria, reduced visual acuity with nystagmus, and bowel and bladder dysfunction.
The single causative gene at the SPG16 locus has not been unequivocally identified, so diagnosis rests on the phenotype, an X-linked pedigree pattern, and exclusion of other defined loci.
Onset in the complicated form is typically early, from infancy to childhood, with slowly progressive lower-limb spasticity and weakness.
Distinguish it from the well-characterised X-linked subtypes SPG1 (L1CAM) and SPG2 (PLP1, allelic to Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease), for which specific gene testing is available.
Lower-limb spasticity with hyperreflexia and extensor plantar responses dominates the motor picture, with relative sparing of the upper limbs.
Sphincter disturbance, including urinary urgency and constipation, is a notable feature of the complicated phenotype and warrants specific enquiry.
Management is symptomatic and multidisciplinary; no disease-modifying therapy exists.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG16 is an X-linked recessive form of hereditary spastic paraplegia linked to the proximal long-arm region Xq11.2-q23. As in the wider HSP group, the core lesion is a length-dependent, retrograde ('dying-back') degeneration of the longest corticospinal tract axons and, to a lesser degree, the dorsal columns, producing progressive lower-limb spasticity and weakness. Unlike the well-defined X-linked subtypes SPG1 (L1CAM) and SPG2 (PLP1), the causative gene at the SPG16 locus has not been unequivocally identified, so the molecular mechanism is inferred rather than proven; candidate processes include disrupted axonal transport, abnormal myelination or defective membrane trafficking, all recurring themes across the HSPs. The complicated phenotype, with cognitive impairment, aphasia, visual failure with nystagmus and sphincter dysfunction, indicates that the underlying defect is not confined to the corticospinal system but affects broader central nervous system development and maintenance. Male hemizygotes are affected, whereas heterozygous females are typically spared or only subtly symptomatic owing to random X-inactivation.
additionalDifferentials: SPG1 (L1CAM) - X-linked, part of the L1 syndrome spectrum with hydrocephalus and adducted thumbs
SPG2 (PLP1) - X-linked, allelic to Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease with central hypomyelination
SPG24, SPG27 and SPG28 - autosomal recessive early-onset complicated or pure sibling subtypes
Adrenomyeloneuropathy (X-linked, ABCD1) - screened by very-long-chain fatty acids
Arginase deficiency - a treatable metabolic mimic of childhood spastic diplegia
Dopa-responsive dystonia - a treatable mimic that must be excluded
Spastic diplegic cerebral palsy - non-progressive, in contrast to the progressive course of HSP
additionalInvestigations: MRI of brain and whole spine to exclude structural, compressive and demyelinating disease; complicated forms may show white-matter change or a thin corpus callosum
Detailed X-linked pedigree analysis with targeted or panel next-generation sequencing covering known SPG loci
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to detect any associated peripheral neuropathy
Very-long-chain fatty acids to exclude adrenomyeloneuropathy
Plasma amino acids and ammonia to exclude arginase deficiency and related metabolic mimics
Ophthalmological assessment of visual acuity, nystagmus and fundi
Neuropsychological evaluation and formal continence assessment where the complicated phenotype is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness or a sensory level suggesting a compressive or structural myelopathy rather than HSP
Acute rather than insidious onset of bladder or bowel dysfunction
Marked asymmetry or prominent upper-limb involvement pointing to an alternative diagnosis
Developmental regression or seizures suggesting a broader neurometabolic disorder
reference.prognosis: The course is slowly progressive, and many affected males retain ambulation with walking aids for years. The complicated form carries greater disability because of the additional cognitive, visual and sphincter involvement, and there is no curative treatment.
pitfalls: Assuming a confirmatory molecular test exists - the SPG16 gene is not definitively established, so a negative gene panel does not exclude the diagnosis
Mislabelling early-onset cases as cerebral palsy, which is static, whereas HSP is progressive
Settling on HSP before excluding treatable mimics such as arginase deficiency and dopa-responsive dystonia
Attributing subtle signs in carrier females to an unrelated cause rather than skewed X-inactivation
